slides.title: What about motion?

elements.text: The noise is the big input.

slides.speech: Then video models showed up, and the gap got worse. Say I want this orange cat to yawn. I can type “the cat yawns,” but text can't say when, how wide, or which way. The model makes that up. But a video model doesn't start from text. It starts from this: random static, one block per frame. That noise already decides a lot. Same prompt, different noise, different video. So what if the noise itself moved?

slides.title: Remember the RickRoll?

elements.text: Every single frame is still pure static.

slides.speech: Remember the RickRoll from the start? That was it. Left, the input video. Middle, its optical flow, which way each pixel moves to the next frame. Right, our warped noise, where every speck travels along that flow. Any single frame is pure static. Only over time can you see Rick. That correlation across time is the control signal.

slides.title: Just warp it?
slides.speech: Why not warp the noise like an image? Top left, a roller coaster zooming forward. Top right, nearest-neighbor copies the same noise pixel into streaks. Bottom left, bilinear averages neighbors: average four unit-variance values and you get variance one quarter, so it goes gray, and neighbors share inputs, so it goes blurry. Moran's I, the spatial correlation, is 0.26 and 0.30, p of zero. Ours is 0.0001, p 0.84, same as fresh noise. And the model notices: in DeepFloyd super-resolution, bilinear noise doubles LPIPS, 0.29 to 0.60.

slides.title: Noise as particles

elements.text: If frame t is i.i.d. Gaussian, so is t+1.

slides.speech: So how? Treat each noise pixel as a particle with a density p, starting at one. Green arrows push particles forward along the flow; three land on q-prime-two. The orange pixels are holes nobody landed on, so the blue arrows pull from q-two along the backward flow. Now q-two has three edges, and here's the trick: every source splits into one independent piece per edge, contraction edge included, using conditional sampling from How I Warped Your Noise. Each piece is used exactly once. So q-prime-two gets one third of q-two, its density is seven thirds, and the holes get one third each. Still four total. Each target sums its pieces weighted by density and divides by the standard deviation. No two output pixels share randomness, so if frame t is i.i.d. Gaussian, so is t plus one. It's linear in pixels per frame, 2 milliseconds at 1024 squared, 26 times faster than How I Warped Your Noise.

slides.title: Just swap the noise
slides.speech: Why fine-tune? Feed warped noise to untuned CogVideoX and the motion roughly follows, but frames fall apart: it's never seen correlated noise. So we warp noise for four million videos and train with CogVideoX's own code. The only change is which noise goes in. A rank-2048 LoRA, 40 A100-days. Motion is seen at the latent's resolution, 8 by 8 pixels, every fourth frame. We also blend in fresh noise by a random gamma; lower gamma is stricter, about 0.5 for drags, lower for transfer. Now drag a polygon on the cat, copy a video's camera, or spin a 3D blob into a squirrel. On DAVIS, motion tracking mIoU goes from 0.52 with plain CogVideoX to 0.74. On our own 40 examples, people picked ours over SG-I2V, MotionClone and DragAnything 82% of the time.

slides.title: What became of it

elements.text: DMT wins text-to-video motion transfer: 0.85 vs 0.70
Motion under 8 px or 4 frames is lost
2D flow can't say occlusion or new stuff

slides.speech: It has limits. DMT optimizes per video and beats us on text-to-video motion transfer, 0.85 versus 0.70. Anything smaller than the latent grid is lost. Flow is 2D, so it can't say what's behind something or what appears. And every base model needs its own fine-tune. Still, it was a CVPR oral, and follow-ups like WonderPlay use it as their motion-to-video stage. But it makes new videos. What if you already have one and want to change how things move in it?
